questions.question_text: Cotherapy is most often used with
questions.explanation: Cotherapy is often used in groups treating substance abuse[cite: 12]. There are many problems that involve the family of substance abusers and require attention on the part of the group leader[cite: 12]. Extragroup issues, including legal problems, debt, housing, and employment, are all factors that affect conducting a group composed of substance abusers[cite: 12]. Staff burnout is high among those who work exclusively with the problems of substance abuse[cite: 12]. Team leadership is advantageous in allowing for the sharing of leadership tasks in the group[cite: 12]. Having more than one leader increases options for identification, interaction, and the exploration of intragroup relationships[cite: 12]. The leader’s therapeutic load is then lightened as a result, and the pace of the group can be accelerated[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Which of the following methods is not used in biofeed- back?
questions.explanation: A strain gauge is a device for measuring nocturnal penile tumescence that is used to determine whether erections occur during sleep[cite: 12]. It has no biofeedback applications[cite: 12]. In electromyography, muscle fibers generate electrical potentials that can be measured on an electromyograph[cite: 12]. Electrodes placed in or on a specific muscle group can be monitored for relaxation training[cite: 12]. In electroencephalography (EEG), the evoked potential of the EEG is monitored to determine relaxation[cite: 12]. In galvanic skin response, skin conductance of electricity is measured as an indicator of autonomic nervous system activity[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Flooding

options.text: is indicated in anxious patients who are psychologi- cally fragile because of its rapid response rate

questions.explanation: Flooding works best with specific phobias, such as a social fear of eating in public[cite: 12].It is sometimes called “implosion” and is similar to graded exposure in that it involves exposing the patient to the feared object in vivo; however, there is no hierarchy[cite: 12]. It is based on the premise that escaping from an anxiety-provoking experience reinforces the anxiety through conditioning[cite: 12]. Thus, clinicians can extinguish the anxiety and prevent the conditioned avoidance behavior by not allowing the patient to escape the situation[cite: 12]. Patients are exposed to the feared situation with no buildup, and no relaxation techniques are used[cite: 12]. Patients experience fear, which gradually subsides over time[cite: 12]. Many patients refuse it because of the psychological discomfort involved, and it is contraindicated when intense anxiety would be hazardous to a patient, such as those who are psychologically fragile[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Dialectical behavior therapy

options.text: does not directly target suicidal behavior
has not been empirically evaluated for efficacy
favors inpatient treatment when self-destructive risk is high

questions.explanation: Dialectical behavior therapy is a cognitive behavioral treatment program that also draws on methods from supportive therapies, as well as some Eastern philosophical schools, such as Zen Buddhism[cite: 12]. It does not focus on insight[cite: 12]. It has been developed to treat suicidal patients who meet criteria for borderline personality disorder and has been evaluated empirically[cite: 12]. A recent study has demonstrated that it directly targets suicidal behavior[cite: 12]. An important strategy of dialectical behavior therapy is to encourage outpatient use of behavioral skills over inpatient treatment even when self-destructive or suicidal risk is high[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not part of the initial phase of interpersonal psychotherapy?

options.text: Give a name and information on the prevalence and characteristics of the disorder.
Describe the rationale and nature of the therapy.
Identify the current interpersonal problem area(s) associated with the onset of symptoms.
Implement strategies specific to identified problem areas.
Review significant relationships, past and present.

correct_answer.text: Implement strategies specific to identified problem areas.

correct_answers.text: Implement strategies specific to identified problem areas.

questions.explanation: The initial phase is dedicated to identifying the problem area that will be the target for treatment[cite: 12]. The intermediate phase is devoted to working on the target problem area(s)[cite: 12]. The termination phase is focused on consolidating gains made during treatment and preparing the patient for future work on his or her own (Table 34.1)[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Supportive psychotherapy

options.text: involves deep exploration of the past
involves the judicious suspension of therapeutic neu- trality
places major etiological emphasis on intrapsychic events
is indicated primarily for patients whose potential for decompensation is low

correct_answer.text: involves the judicious suspension of therapeutic neu- trality

correct_answers.text: involves the judicious suspension of therapeutic neu- trality

questions.explanation: Supportive psychotherapy aims at the creation of a therapeutic relationship as a temporary bridge for the deficient patient[cite: 12]. Techniques are designed to focus on conscious external events and on the therapist as a largely nontransferential figure[cite: 12]. As such, therapeutic neutrality is judiciously suspended with much greater direction, disclosure, and gratification offered than would be appropriate in other approaches[cite: 12]. The global perspective of supportive psychotherapy places major etiological emphasis on external rather than intrapsychic events, particularly on stressful environmental and interpersonal influences on a damaged self[cite: 12]. It is indicated generally for those whose potential for decompensation is high (not low)[cite: 12]. It focuses on the here and now of the patient’s problems; genetic interpretations relating to the patient’s past may cause decompensation and are generally contraindicated in this treatment[cite: 12]. The therapist works to diminish the breakthrough of regressive transferences[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Brief focal psychotherapy

options.text: is very helpful for self-destructive acting-out patients
involves setting a termination date in advance
usually lasts less than 10 to 12 sessions

correct_answer.text: involves setting a termination date in advance

correct_answers.text: involves setting a termination date in advance

questions.explanation: Brief focal psychotherapy was originally developed in the 1950s at the Tavistock Clinic in London[cite: 12]. In it, the therapist formulates a circumscribed focus and sets a termination date in advance[cite: 12]. Contraindications to this treatment include grossly destructive acting-out patients, patients who are chronically dependent on alcohol or other substances of abuse, and patients with a history of serious suicide attempts[cite: 12]. The therapist identifies the transference early and interprets it[cite: 12]. Both the patient and the therapist become deeply involved, and the therapist does not remain detached[cite: 12]. An experienced therapist allows about 20 sessions as an average length for the therapy[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: An interpersonal psychotherapist is presented with a patient who was married 9 months prior and is having difficulty adapting to married life. The goals of therapy for this patient include

options.text: accepting the loss of the single life
recognizing the positive as well as the negative as- pects of being married
developing a sense of mastery regarding the demands of married life
understanding the cause of the distress

questions.explanation: In the initial phase of interpersonal psychotherapy, the problem area for the patient is identified, and specific goals for treatment of the problem area are set[cite: 12]. The identified problem area for the aforementioned patient is role transition[cite: 12]. Role transition includes any difficulties resulting from a change in life status[cite: 12]. For this patient, the change is marriage[cite: 12]. The goals of therapy include (1) mourning and accepting the loss of the old role (in this case, the patient’s life as a single person), (2) recognizing the positive and negative aspects of both the old role (being single) and the new role (being married), and (3) restoring the patient’s self-esteem by developing a sense of mastery in the demands of the new role (married life)[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: A spiritual assessment

options.text: involves learning about the patient’s beliefs
empowers the patient to find inner resources of strength
is completed during the social history section of the history and physical examination

questions.explanation: The spiritual history is taken during the social history section of the history and physical examination[cite: 12]. The goals of the spiritual history are to invite the patient to share spiritual and religious beliefs if he or she chooses to do so; to learn about the patient’s beliefs and values; to assess for spiritual distress, such as meaninglessness as well as for spiritual resources of strength; to provide an opportunity for compassionate care whereby the health care professional connects to the patient in a deep and profound way; to empower the patient to find inner resources of healing and acceptance; and to learn about the patient’s spiritual and religious beliefs that might affect health care decision making[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: In combined individual and group therapy, patients with which of the following disorders are at a higher risk of playing off one therapy against the other?
questions.explanation:
In combined individual and group therapy, a patient with a borderline or narcissistic personality disorder is at higher risk to play off one therapy against the other as a resistance to change[cite: 12]. Astute uses of combined therapy can identify this dysfunctional behavior and offer more-adaptive alternatives[cite: 12]. Specifically, a personality-disordered patient in combined therapy may use individual therapy to focus on intrapsychic issues and can apply the insights gained in therapy and experiment with new modes of behavior in the safe and controlled interpersonal setting of the group[cite: 12].
Paranoid personality disorder is characterized by rigidity, hypersensitivity, unwarranted suspicion, jealousy, envy, an exaggerated sense of importance, and a tendency to blame and ascribe evil motives[cite: 12]. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is characterized by perfectionism, overconscientiousness, and excessive inhibition with regard to self-expression and relaxation[cite: 12]. Schizoid personality disorder is diagnosed for persons who are unable to form social relationships but without other striking communicative or behavioral eccentricities[cite: 12]. Schizotypal personality disorder is diagnosed for persons who exhibit various eccentricities in communication or behavior coupled with defects in the capacity to form social relationships[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Systematic desensitization is applicable in the treatment of
questions.explanation:
Systematic desensitization is applicable in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), sexual disorders, stuttering, bronchial asthma, and other conditions[cite: 12]. Joseph Wolpe first described systematic desensitization, a behavioral technique in which the patient is trained in muscle relaxation, and then a hierarchy of anxiety-provoking thoughts or objects is paired with the relaxed state until the anxiety is systematically decreased and eliminated[cite: 12].
Through systematic desensitization, patients with OCD can be conditioned not to feel anxious when around those objects or situations causing anxiety[cite: 12]. Desensitization has been used effectively with some stutterers by deconditioning the anxiety associated with a range of speaking situations[cite: 12]. Some sexual disorders—such as male orgasmic disorder, female orgasmic disorder, and premature ejaculation—are amenable to desensitization therapy[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: The goals of social skills training include all of the following except

options.text: generalization of the acquired skills to similar situa- tions
acquisition of insight into the social deficit

correct_answer.text: acquisition of insight into the social deficit

correct_answers.text: acquisition of insight into the social deficit

questions.explanation: Social skills are interpersonal behaviors required for community survival; independence; and establishing, maintaining, and deepening supportive, socially rewarding relationships[cite: 12]. Severe mental disorders such as schizophrenia disrupt one or more affective, cognitive, behavioral, and verbal domains of functioning and impair the patient’s potential for enjoying and sustaining interpersonal relationships[cite: 12]. Social skills training is a psychosocial rehabilitative treatment designed to remediate deficits in social behaviors[cite: 12]. It does not address understanding or insight and focuses on the behaviors themselves[cite: 12]. The major goals of social skills training include improved social skills in specific situations, generalization of the acquired skills to similar situations, acquisition or relearning of social and conversational skills, and decreased social anxiety[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: A physician who practices positive psychology gives a patient the following exercise: Every night for 1 week, set aside 10 minutes before you go to bed. Use that time to write down three things that went really well on that day and why they went well. You may use a journal or your computer to write about the events, but it is important that you have a physical record of what you wrote. It is not enough to do this exercise in your head. The three things listed can be relatively small in importance or relatively large in importance. Next to each positive event in your list, answer the question, “Why did this good thing happen?” In positive psychology, this exercise is used to
questions.explanation: Positive psychologists have demonstrated that brief interventions in the short term can increase happiness, satisfaction, and fulfillment[cite: 12]. For example, patients can be asked to count their blessings, as in this case, to increase life satisfaction[cite: 12]. In some cases, there is also evidence that brief interventions can alleviate depression[cite: 12]. Table 34.2 provides examples of positive psychology techniques and interventions[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Charles was a 70-year-old retired business executive. Throughout his life, his work consumed him. Although he was married and had a family, his job was his primary focus. He went to the office early and came home late. But as he got older, his performance at work was not what it used to be, and he decided it was time to retire. However, his mood was pretty low when he no longer had a job. The therapist spent some time with Charles talking about the kinds of activities that used to make him feel good and some of the things he used to enjoy. They then put together a list of things he might be able to do—even if he did not feel much like it—just to see what would happen. The list included looking for volunteer work where he could use his job skills, spending more time with his wife doing some of the activities they once had enjoyed (e.g., watching movies, taking walks), and rejuvenating an old hobby from his college days—fishing. Charles initially agreed to do some easy activities—go to one movie a week, take one walk a week, and contact his church activity leader about possible volunteer activities. This case illustrates which type of behavior therapy technique?
questions.explanation:
Behavioral activation postulates that depression persists because depressed behavior is more highly reinforced than nondepressed behavior[cite: 12]. Positive reinforcement from participation in pleasurable activities results in an increase in positive mood[cite: 12]. In this process, the therapist works with the patient in setting weekly behavioral goals, as with the case of Charles[cite: 12]. Each week, the patient carries out these goals and reports back on the results at the next session[cite: 12]. The more weekly goals are accomplished, the more positive reinforcement reduces the depressive symptoms[cite: 12]. As Charles performed the activities in his weekly list, he found himself feeling better[cite: 12].
Exposure therapy postulates that fears are acquired through associative learning (classical and operative conditioning)[cite: 12]. Interventions to eliminate fear use the same conditioning principles, and elimination of maladaptive fears requires exposure (contact) with the feared object, event, or situation[cite: 12]. Similar to exposure therapies, aversion-based approaches consist of different interventions[cite: 12]. Some are based on operant principles, and others are based on counterconditioning strategies[cite: 12].
Contingency management is defined as the general application of operant principles (e.g., reinforcement, punishment) in the process of behavior change[cite: 12]. When used efficiently, contingency management procedures can terminate negative reinforcement cycles, clarify behavioral expectations, and teach people how to bargain and compromise rather than resort to coercive procedures and how to define and clarify what they want and expect[cite: 12].
Although many behavioral treatments involve some elements of self-control, as patients take responsibility for changing behaviors, more direct self-control approaches are defined by the use of stimuli, behaviors, and consequences with oneself to achieve a desired outcome[cite: 12]. Common self-control strategies include physically restraining oneself, chaining the stimuli conditions, depriving or satiating oneself, and administering self-reinforcement or self-punishment[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Focuses on a person’s differentiation from his or her family of origin
questions.explanation: The hallmark of the Bowen model is a person’s differentiation from his or her family of origin[cite: 12]. This involves the person’s ability to be his or her true self in the face of familial or other pressures that threaten the loss of love or social position[cite: 12]. In a structural model, families are viewed as single, interrelated systems, assessed in terms of significant alliances and splits among family members, hierarchy of power, boundaries among generations, and family tolerance for each other[cite: 12]. Psychodynamic-experiential models emphasize individual maturation in the context of the family system and freedom from unconscious patterns of anxiety and projection rooted in the past[cite: 12]. The general systems model is based on general systems theory, a model that holds that families are systems and that every action in a family produces a reaction in one or more of its members[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Patient’s agreement to tell the therapist everything with- out selection
questions.explanation: In free association, patients say whatever comes to mind[cite: 12]. This is in compliance with the fundamental rule of psychoanalysis, in which the patient agrees to be completely honest with the analyst and to tell everything without selection[cite: 12]. Inevitably, the patient cannot accomplish this task, and these constitute resistances to the process[cite: 12]. Resistances prevent unconscious ideas or feelings from being experienced consciously[cite: 12]. The analyst’s counterpart to the patient’s free association is a particular way of listening, referred to as free-floating or evenly suspended attention[cite: 12]. The therapeutic or working alliance refers to the relationship established by the patient and analyst that involves two adults embarking on a joint venture, involving mutual trust, cooperation, and an endeavor to explore the patient’s symptoms to achieve amelioration of those symptoms[cite: 12].
